title: What Tor Carries

pages.text:
*From the Walk-Book of Highstep, Day 14. Weather: fair. Distance: three miles. Direction: left. The goats are unpacked. The Mayor is not speaking to the goats.*

The errand was simple, which was why Mo did not like it. Mrs. Pell’s knees ached from the storm, and she wanted a sack of the soft, spongy moss that grew only in the Fold. Getting there meant climbing down a narrow chute of rock between the pine roots. The rope bridges avoided this place for good reason. It was damp, dark, and smelled of wet stone and old rain.

Mo went first. His bare feet found purchase on the slick lichen. Junie followed, her tool-belt clinking against the rock face. "Careful," she said, her voice echoing weirdly in the hollow space. "If you slip, you’ll go all the way down. I don’t think there’s a net."

"There’s no net," Mo agreed, pressing one heel into the groove of a root. He felt a faint vibration, a low thrum from deep within the mountain’s shoulder. Tor seemed calm here, almost sleepy, her heat radiating up through the rock. "She likes it down here. It’s like a pocket."

The air grew warmer as they descended, thick with the scent of crushed ferns. Glowing blue lichen dotted the walls, pulsing softly in the dim light. It was quiet down there. A silence that felt held in, waiting. Mo looked back at the shaft of daylight far above, then at Junie, who was checking her nails for sharpness. She looked nervous. He wanted to say something to make it better. But the moss was calling to him, soft and green and waiting.
pages.image: Two children descend a narrow rock chute into a dark, mossy hollow; blue lichen glows on the walls, and warm damp air rises from the earth below while pine roots frame the path.

pages.text:
They dropped onto a bed of ferns so dense it swallowed their boots, if they had worn them. The Fold was a hidden room in the mountain’s side, a cavern of dripping stone and ancient shadow. But it was the walls that stopped Mo cold.

Carvings. Dozens of them, scratched deep into the grey rock.

Junie ran her hand along the surface, her fingers tracing the grooves with a builder’s precision. "Tally marks," she said, her voice hushed. "Groups of five. Hundreds of them." She turned to Mo, her eyes wide behind her spectacles. "That’s not decoration. That’s a count."

Mo stepped closer. He did not read the marks; he felt them. He pressed his palm flat against the stone, feeling the vibration of the cuts. They were old, worn smooth by time, but the intent was there, sharp and deliberate. And there were other things, too. Handprints. Tiny ones, no bigger than a child’s palm, pressed into the rock.

"Somebody was here," Mo whispered. "Before us."

Junie looked at the handprints, then at the small, intricate figures carved beside them: stick people with tools, with ropes, with goats. "They were just like us," she said. "Living on the back. Keeping count."
pages.image: Two children examine ancient carvings on a stone wall; tiny handprints and tally marks are etched into the rock, illuminated by soft blue lichen light and the children's lanterns.

pages.text:
The row of handprints stretched along the wall, one for every year of the Long Walk, creating a long, unbroken line of history that felt heavier than any stack of books. Mo followed it with his eyes, counting the gaps where the stone was too worn to see, until the shapes seemed to flow into the dark like a river of small, silent voices. Then, at the very end of the row, the carving changed completely.

It was not a handprint. It was a scene.

A mountain, huge and grey, lay down. Not walking, not standing, but resting. Above it, a wide curve of water was drawn with a single, confident line. In the foreground, a crowd of tiny figures stood on the shore, holding hands in a circle that looked familiar, like the way Gran and Mo held hands when they walked the rope bridges at dusk.

Junie stared. Her breath hitched, a small, sharp sound in the quiet cave. "Mo," she said, her voice barely a whisper. "This is the drawing."

Mo looked at the carving, then at Junie. The image in his mind from the library, the faded drawing with its strange, unfinished edge, matched the rock perfectly. The mountain was not lost. It was going somewhere. Somewhere with a shore.
pages.image: Two children stare at a detailed carving on a stone wall showing a mountain lying down under a curve of water, with tiny figures holding hands on the shore below.

pages.text:
"Maybe that’s what happens," Junie said. She did not look at Mo. Instead, her eyes stayed fixed on the carving, her face tight and careful, like a child trying not to cry in front of a teacher. "When it stops. It gets a shore. A house that stays."

Mo felt a cold prickle at the back of his neck. "I don’t want a shore," he said, pressing one bare heel into the stone floor to steady himself. "I want Highstep."

"Highstep is just a word," Junie replied, and this time she turned to face him. Her voice was sharp, but her hands were trembling against her leather tool-belt, the nails clinking softly. "It’s just a group of houses on a moving thing. If the thing stops, the houses are still there. But they’re different. They’re... still."

Mo heard the words, but he did not hear the shake underneath, the fear that lived in her throat, the terror of a floor that would finally stop tilting. He wanted to reach out and hold her hand, to tell her that Highstep was the people, not the place. But the words stuck in his mouth, heavy and useless, like a mouthful of dry hay. The mountain hummed, low and deep, a sound that vibrated in his bones. It was not sad. It was waiting.
pages.image: Two children stand in a dim cave, one looking at the other with concern, the other staring at a stone wall, their faces lit by faint blue light from glowing lichen.

pages.text:
They climbed back up the chute in silence. The air grew cooler as they ascended, the smell of the deep Fold fading, replaced by the scent of pine needles and wet earth. When Mo emerged into the light, the sun was high and bright, the sky a pale, washed-out blue.

Admiral was waiting on a flat rock above them. He was chewing on something. He looked at Mo, his one crooked horn tilted, and swallowed. Then, with a soft *thump*, a crumpled piece of paper fell from his mouth.

Mo frowned. He walked over and picked it up. It was torn, stained with grass and goat drool. But it was not just scrap. It was a map. A map of the ground ahead. A river, a plain, and far away, a thin, blue line that looked like water.

Junie took it from him, her hands shaking. "He’s been eating it," she said. "He’s been saving it for us."
pages.image: A large brown and white goat with one crooked horn stands on a rock, having just dropped a torn piece of paper at the feet of two children who look up in surprise.
